content.title: About
content.content: Caviar is the salt-cured roe (eggs) of sturgeon and, more broadly, other fish such as salmon, trout, and whitefish. It is a delicacy made of small, glossy, pearl-like eggs with a rich, briny, buttery flavor. Caviar is usually eaten cold in small amounts, on its own or as a topping on blini, toast, and eggs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: True caviar comes from sturgeon, while roe from salmon, trout, and other fish is also sold as caviar or red caviar.
Caviar is made by gently removing the eggs from the fish, rinsing them, and curing them with salt.
Traditionally, caviar is served with a non-metallic spoon, such as mother-of-pearl, bone, or plastic, to avoid altering its flavor.
Many wild sturgeon species are endangered, so most caviar today comes from farmed sturgeon.
Caviar is a delicacy in Russia, Iran, and across Europe and is traditionally served at celebrations.

items.title: Source of omega-3 fatty acids
items.content: Fish roe provides EPA and DHA, which support normal heart and brain function.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Provides protein
items.content: Caviar provides protein, although it is eaten in small amounts.

items.title: Provides selenium, iron, and vitamin D
items.content: Fish roe provides selenium, iron, and some vitamin D.

items.title: Contains choline
items.content: Caviar contains choline, which supports normal cell function.

items.title: Very high in sodium
items.content: Caviar is cured with salt and can be very high in sodium, so people limiting salt should eat it sparingly.

items.title: Cholesterol and purines
items.content: Caviar contains cholesterol and purines, which matters for people with certain health conditions such as gout.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Caviar can cause allergic reactions in people allergic to fish.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Refrigerated, unpasteurized caviar can carry Listeria and is not recommended for pregnant women, young children, older adults, or people with weakened immunity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Caviar is eaten cold, in small portions, on its own from a non-metallic spoon, or on blini, toast, boiled eggs, potatoes, or with sour cream. Do not cook it or mash it. Lightly chilled caviar and neutral accompaniments let its flavor show.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep caviar in the coldest part of the refrigerator, usually about 0 to 4 °C (32 to 39 °F), and follow the date on the tin or jar. Once opened, press plastic wrap against the surface, close tightly, and eat it within two to three days. Do not freeze it, since freezing damages its texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg, whole, baked, no salt (NS) is a whole chicken egg cooked in the oven without added salt. Baking retains most nutrients while giving the egg a firmer texture compared with boiled eggs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Baked eggs are often used in salads and sandwiches as a convenient protein source.
During baking, the egg white coagulates at a lower temperature than the yolk, leaving the yolk creamy.
Salt‑free eggs are suitable for low‑sodium diets.
Properly cooled baked eggs can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.
Heat treatment destroys most pathogens, including Salmonella.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: One large egg provides about 6 g of complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: The yolk contains vitamin D, which supports bone health and immune function.

items.title: Contains choline
items.content: Choline is important for brain function and fat metabolism.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: No added salt makes this product suitable for people monitoring sodium intake.

items.title: Eye health support
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in the yolk help protect eyes from age‑related degeneration.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins, which can be severe.

items.title: Salmonella risk
items.content: Undercooked eggs may harbor Salmonella; ensure the yolk is fully set.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: The yolk contains cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume in moderation.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A large egg contains about 70 kcal; consider total calories in a balanced diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Baked eggs can be eaten plain, sliced into salads, added to sandwiches, or used as a topping for vegetable dishes. They store well in the fridge and reheat quickly in the microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool baked eggs to room temperature, then keep them in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen yogurt with chocolate is a frozen dessert made from yogurt base and enriched with dark chocolate pieces or glaze. It combines the light tang of yogurt with the rich flavor of chocolate, offering a creamy texture and lower fat content compared to traditional ice cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frozen yogurt originated in the United States in the 1970s as a healthier alternative to ice cream.
Chocolate is often added as chips, a coating, or protein‑rich chocolate balls.
The yogurt base provides probiotics that support gut health.
In Russia, frozen yogurt’s popularity is rising thanks to a wide range of flavors and low calorie count.
The yogurt‑chocolate combo is frequently used in sports nutrition for post‑workout recovery.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: The yogurt base contains live cultures that help maintain a healthy digestive system.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with regular ice cream, frozen yogurt typically contains less fat, making it a lighter dessert option.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Yogurt provides a good amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Antioxidants from chocolate
items.content: Dark chocolate is high in flavonoids, which help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy support
items.content: The mix of carbohydrates and protein in yogurt offers a quick and sustained energy boost.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Yogurt contains lactose, so individuals with intolerance should choose lactose‑free versions.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some people may be allergic to casein or whey proteins present in yogurt.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: Certain frozen yogurt products may contain added sugars; checking the label is advisable.

items.title: Caffeine in chocolate
items.content: Dark chocolate contains small amounts of caffeine, which can affect sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is sold in single‑serve cups or cones. It can be eaten straight from the container, or topped with fresh berries, nuts, or honey for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen yogurt at –18 °C or lower. After opening, consume within 2–3 days, storing it in an airtight container in the freezer to prevent ice crystal formation.

grilled-cheese-sandwich-cheddar-cheese-o.title: Grilled cheese sandwich, cheddar cheese, on wheat bread

content.title: About
content.content: A grilled cheese sandwich is a hot sandwich made with slices of wheat bread buttered on the outside and filled with melted cheddar cheese, toasted on a skillet or grill until the bread is golden and the cheese becomes gooey.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first grilled cheese recipes appeared in the United States in the early 1920s.
Cheddar originated in the English county of Somerset and is now one of the world’s most popular cheeses.
Wheat bread adds extra fiber and slower‑digesting carbs compared with white bread.
Traditionally the sandwich is fried in butter, but olive oil can be used for a lighter flavor.
In the U.S., grilled cheese is often served with tomato soup.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cheddar provides a good amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Cheddar supplies high‑quality animal protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 in cheese supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of carbs from bread and fats from cheese gives a quick source of energy.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: Certain aged cheddars contain live cultures that may benefit gut health.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheddar can trigger allergic reactions in people with dairy allergies or lactose intolerance.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese often contains a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Grilled cheese is relatively high in calories; portion control is advised for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Trans fats in cooking oil
items.content: Using oils high in trans fats for frying can increase cardiovascular risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sandwich hot, cut diagonally. It can be paired with tomato soup, ham, avocado, or fresh vegetables. For a lighter version, use whole‑grain bread and reduced‑fat cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Grilled cheese is best eaten immediately. If you need to store it, let it cool to room temperature, wrap tightly in foil, and refrigerate for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a toaster oven or skillet before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: A light orange juice beverage contains 40‑50 % natural orange juice diluted with water and lightly sweetened. It offers a bright citrus flavor, mild carbonation and low calories, making it a popular refreshing choice in warm weather.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Orange juice is one of the most consumed fruit juices worldwide.
A 40‑50 % juice content balances the taste of real juice with a lighter texture.
The drink retains vitamins C and A, though in lower amounts than pure juice.
Light fruit beverages often use natural flavorings instead of artificial ones.
In many countries these drinks are classified as “juice drinks,” not pure juice.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: The beverage provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The water component helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Low Calorie
items.content: Because the juice is diluted, the drink has fewer calories than pure juice, useful for weight management.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: It contains potassium, important for normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids present in orange juice have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Sugar Content
items.content: Despite being light, the beverage still contains added sugar, which may be undesirable for diabetics or those limiting sugar intake.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidity of orange juice can irritate the stomach lining in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Citrus Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to citrus.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some versions may contain preservatives that not everyone tolerates well.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the beverage chilled as a refreshing drink throughout the day, use it in cocktails, smoothies, or as a base for fruit punches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Pancakes, fruit, frozen are a ready‑to‑cook product consisting of thin pancakes that already contain pieces of berries and fruit. They are convenient to store in the freezer and can be quickly prepared on a skillet or in a microwave. The taste combines the softness of the batter with the sweet‑tart flavor of the fruit.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pancakes are often used as a quick breakfast or snack.
Typical fruit additions include strawberry, blueberry, banana and mango.
Freezing preserves most of the vitamins thanks to rapid flash‑freezing.
The classic pancake recipe originates from French crêpes.
In some countries they are served with yogurt or ice cream.

items.title: Source of vitamins
items.content: The fruit component provides vitamin C and vitamin A, which support immunity and vision.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Fruit fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The batter is prepared with minimal added oil, making the product suitable for moderate fat intake.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates from the batter and fruit quickly replenish glycogen stores, useful before exercise.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Berries contain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The batter may contain wheat, so people with celiac disease should choose a gluten‑free version.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fruit additions can raise sugar levels, which is important for individuals with diabetes.

items.title: Additive concerns
items.content: Some manufacturers add preservatives; check the ingredient list if you are sensitive to food additives.

items.title: Risk of under‑heating
items.content: If not heated properly, the pancakes may remain cold inside, increasing the risk of food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Defrost the pancakes in the microwave or on a skillet, then serve with yogurt, honey, nuts or fresh berries. They can also be used as a base for dessert rolls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen pancakes in an airtight bag at –18 °C or lower. After thawing, consume within 24 hours and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Venison is lean meat from deer, obtained through hunting or farming. It has a delicate flavor, a slightly sweet aroma, and a firm yet tender texture. Venison is rich in protein, iron, zinc, and B‑vitamins while being low in fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Venison is considered one of the most diet‑friendly meats because of its low fat content.
Traditional cuisines in Scandinavia, Russia, and Canada use venison in stews, sausages, and dried meat products.
Deer feed on a wide variety of vegetation, giving the meat a unique taste that changes with season and region.
In some cultures venison symbolizes strength and endurance.
Dried venison jerky can be stored for several months without refrigeration.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Venison provides about 22 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with beef, venison contains only 2–3 % fat, making it suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Rich source of iron
items.content: Heme iron from venison is highly bioavailable, helping to prevent anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies B12, B6, and niacin, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals: zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace elements are important for immune health and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Parasite contamination risk
items.content: Raw or undercooked venison may contain parasites such as Trichinella; thorough cooking is essential.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: People prone to gout should limit excessive venison consumption.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may be allergic to wild game meat.

items.title: Sodium in processed products
items.content: Venison sausages and cured jerky are often salted, increasing sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Venison can be grilled, roasted, braised, or pan‑seared. Marinating in an acidic medium (wine, vinegar) for a few hours helps tenderize the meat. It is used for steaks, ground meat, sausages, and dried jerky.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh venison in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C for 2–3 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Dried and cured products should be kept in a cool, dry place in a sealed container.
